notes.h: Definitions: chemical cell and fuel cell
points: A chemical cell, e.g. a zinc–carbon, alkaline, lead–acid or lithium-ion cell, uses a redox reaction between reactants sealed inside it to convert chemical energy into electrical energy.
A chemical cell stops working when its reactants have been used up.
When a chemical cell's reactants are used up, a primary cell is discarded, while a secondary cell must be recharged from an external electrical supply.
A fuel cell converts the chemical energy of a fuel, e.g. hydrogen, and an oxidising agent, usually oxygen from the air, into electrical energy.
In a fuel cell the reactants are not stored in the cell but are supplied continuously from outside, and the products, water for hydrogen, are continuously removed.
A fuel cell keeps producing electricity for as long as fuel and oxidant are supplied; it is refuelled, not recharged, and does not run down like a chemical cell.

notes.h: What chemical cells and fuel cells have in common
points: Both are galvanic cells: each uses a spontaneous redox reaction to drive electrons through an external circuit.
Both have an anode where the fuel or reducing agent is oxidised (negative), a cathode where the oxidising agent is reduced (positive), and an electrolyte that carries ions between them.
In both, oxidation and reduction happen at separate electrodes, so energy is released as electrical energy rather than as heat.

notes.h: Chemical cells compared with fuel cells
points: Source of reactants: a chemical cell stores its reactants inside and is limited by them; a fuel cell is supplied continuously from external tanks or the air.
Products: in a chemical cell they stay inside the cell; in a fuel cell they are removed continuously, e.g. as water vapour in the exhaust.
When reactants run out: a chemical cell is replaced (primary) or recharged, which can take hours (secondary); a fuel cell is refuelled in minutes.

Energy storage: in a chemical cell the energy is stored in the electrode materials, so more energy needs a bigger, heavier cell; in a fuel cell the energy is stored in the fuel tank, so the range depends on the size of the tank.

Typical uses: chemical cells power portable devices such as phones, laptops and torches, and battery electric vehicles; fuel cells power hydrogen buses, cars and trucks, spacecraft and backup power supplies.
Environmental impact: a hydrogen fuel cell's only product is water; chemical cells need metals such as lithium, cobalt, nickel, lead and zinc to be mined, and the cells must be recycled.
A fuel cell needs hydrogen to be produced, stored and transported, and is only as clean as the way the hydrogen was made (see "Electrochemistry and sustainability").

notes.h: Fuel cell compared with burning the fuel
points: In a fuel cell hydrogen and oxygen react by the same overall reaction as when hydrogen burns, 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, but without a flame or combustion: the electrons are transferred through the external circuit.

A fuel cell converts chemical energy directly into electrical energy; an engine or power station first converts it to heat, much of which is lost, so a fuel cell is more efficient than burning the fuel.
A fuel cell has no moving parts, so it is quiet.
A hydrogen fuel cell produces no carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide or soot at the point of use and, with no high-temperature flame, no nitrogen oxides.

keyTerms.definition: A cell that converts chemical energy into electrical energy from reactants sealed inside it, and stops when they are used up.
A galvanic cell that converts the chemical energy of a fuel and an oxidising agent into electrical energy, with both supplied continuously from outside.
A substance that is oxidised in a reaction to release energy, such as hydrogen in a fuel cell.
A substance that gains electrons and is reduced in a redox reaction, such as oxygen in a fuel cell.
The burning of a fuel with oxygen, releasing energy as heat and light.
A cell in which a spontaneous redox reaction drives electrons through an external circuit.

questions.prompt: Compare a chemical cell with a fuel cell under the headings: source of reactants, removal of products, what happens when the reactants are used up.
questions.model: Source of reactants: a chemical cell stores its reactants inside the cell, so it is limited by them, whereas a fuel cell is supplied continuously with fuel and oxygen from external tanks or the air. Removal of products: in a chemical cell the products stay inside the cell, whereas in a fuel cell the products, such as water for hydrogen, are removed continuously. When the reactants are used up: a chemical cell stops working and is either discarded (primary) or recharged from an external supply, which can take hours (secondary); a fuel cell keeps working as long as fuel and oxidant are supplied and is refuelled in minutes.

questions.prompt: State one similarity between a chemical cell and a fuel cell, and give two advantages of a hydrogen fuel cell over burning hydrogen in an engine.
questions.model: Similarity: both are galvanic cells, each using a spontaneous redox reaction to drive electrons through an external circuit, with an anode where the fuel is oxidised, a cathode where the oxidising agent is reduced, and an electrolyte between them. Advantage 1: a fuel cell converts chemical energy directly into electrical energy, without first making heat, so it is more efficient than burning hydrogen. Advantage 2: a fuel cell has no moving parts, so it is quiet, and a hydrogen fuel cell produces no carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide or soot at the point of use.
